Multiply your divisions-per-cycle by the time-base $0.50 \text{ ms}$ per division to get the period $T$ in $\text{ms}$, then convert to seconds.
Use $f = 1/T$ for the sound wave and check that $T$ near $1.5 \times 10^{-3} \text{ s}$ gives a frequency in the hundreds of hertz.
walkthrough: Look at the horizontal axis of the CRO trace. One full cycle means peak to next peak, or zero-crossing with same slope to the next one.
On the screen one wavelength occupies 3.0 horizontal divisions. Two peaks are 3 divisions apart.
The time-base is $0.50 \text{ ms}$ per division, so period $T = 3.0 \times 0.50 \text{ ms} = 1.5 \text{ ms}$.
Frequency is $f = 1/T = 1/(1.5 \times 10^{-3}) \approx 667 \text{ Hz}$, about $670 \text{ Hz}$ with sensible precision.
